lines: Wedged behind a row of atlases, a photograph of a granite terrace in bright sun, every wall glittering.
On the back, in pencil: 'Mica, not magic. Gran says it all came out of Rubislaw. Gran says a lot.'
Between two cookbooks, a recipe card for tablet in a neat hand, thumbed soft and speckled with sugar.
Along the bottom: 'Makes one tray. NOT for giving away.' Someone has underlined it twice and someone else has ignored it.
On the mantel, a photograph of a small boat on a doorstep, a shed behind it, and the sea at the end of the square.
A gull sits on the shed roof looking at the camera. The caption reads: 'Fittie, nothing wasted. Including the gull.'
Under a pile of recipe books, a note on the back of a flour bag, written in a hurry.
'Rowies cooling on the sill. Dinna fash, I have counted them. The cat has not been told how many.'
Above the grate, a framed photograph of a civic procession in the street, chains of office glinting in a rare patch of sun.
A banner at the front shows three towers and two leopards. The clerk has labelled it in biro: 'Bon Accord. Mostly.'
Under the pillow, a postcard from home with a picture of a lighthouse on it, folded in half.
'Have you eaten anything green? Have you kicked the bar yet? Your father says hello and wants his good umbrella back.'
Behind the plates, a ship in a bottle, rigging as fine as cobweb, the glue still a bit proud at the neck.
It is not one of the eleven on the shelves. There is a label on the base: 'Number twelve. Do not tell her.'
Propped against the books, a lovespoon carved from a single piece of wood, with a heart and a tiny anchor on the handle.
It is a good deal older than the house. A label in the family hand says: 'Nain's, from before the hiraeth set in.'
Stuck behind a jug on the dresser, a postcard in a young hand: 'Annwyl Nain, I bought you two tea towels with the long name on.'
'I know what you will say. Use them for the Welsh cakes. Love, Sioned. P.S. Do not tell the cat.'
On the mantelpiece, a snapshot of a lanky boy in a rowing skiff on the Avon, grinning, soaked to the elbows.
On the back: 'Fall-in number one. Taken from the bank, before the rescue. Photographer: gran, who was laughing too hard to help.'
Among the astronomy books, a hand-painted glass lantern slide showing a ringed planet and a very small, very pleased man.
The label is in copperplate: 'Georgium Sidus'. Someone has added underneath, in biro: 'Rejected. See Uranus.'
On the shelf, a coronation biscuit tin, lid a bit dented, rattling faintly when you pick it up.
No biscuits inside. It is full of odd buttons, all sizes, and a paper label: 'Bath Olivers, 1950s. Buttons, now.'
Under a revision timetable on the bed, a note from a dad with a pen that is running out.
'Bladud and the pigs are lovely, but please do NOT put them in the essay. Eat something. Dad. P.S. Ask the pigs if you need a reference.'
Behind the clock, a scrap of envelope with a note in thick pencil, long forgotten.
'Back in a wee while.' It is dated three days ago. So far as anyone knows, the wee while has not finished.
On the mantel sits a single iron rivet, mushroom-headed and heavy, used as a paperweight and a conversation piece.
A tag reads: 'Granda's. Caught in the bucket, he says. Never dropped. Never again, mind you, if you ask him why.'
Stuck between the books, a child's school drawing of two big cranes with a hundred scribbled starlets on top.
Under it in wobbly capitals: 'WEE ANE'S PICTURE. THE BIRDS ARE LOUD.' The teacher has added a gold star.
Pinned in the display case, a card of pressed flowers and a fern frond, flattened and brown at the edges.
The label is faded: 'Taken from a fallen frond, with the gardener's blessing. Humidity ruined three hairdos in the process.'
On the shelf, a glass prism from an old lamp, heavy as a brick, throwing a small rainbow whenever the sun catches it.
Beside it a notebook of step counts: 183, 187, 181, 186. A note at the bottom says: 'The stairs are lying.'
Propped on a shelf, a photograph of a woman in a headscarf on a narrowboat, holding a mug and not smiling at all.
Behind her, a heron on the towpath eyeing the biscuits. On the back: 'The cut, a Sunday. Kettle was on.'
On the mantel, a snapshot of a girl wobbling along a canal towpath on a bike with her tongue between her teeth.
A duck stands with great authority beside her. The caption says: 'Inspecting. Not fell in. That came later.'
Under the fruit bowl, a school project draft headed 'CANALS, by a Very Serious Person', with a ruler-drawn map.
The teacher has written on it: 'More than Venice? Source please.' Underneath, in red: 'Gran says so.' A second note: 'Not a source.'
Between a road atlas and a bus timetable, a Dinky toy bus, paint worn off at the nose from years of enthusiastic braking.
A scrap of paper tucked inside the stairs reads: 'Number 11. The long way round. Always the long way round.'
Propped against the flour jars, a faded photograph of a young man in his best on a horse, with a crowd and a flag behind.
On the back, in careful ink: 'Cornet, '62. Rode every march. The horse lost. We do not say which.'
Slipped inside a book, an old photograph of a tram on a country road, passengers on top, a dog running alongside.
On the back, shakily: 'Told you. The river did it. Granda.' Someone has underlined 'river' three times.
Between two bird guides, a postcard of a ruined castle on a cliff, sent by a friend with a very bad sense of humour.
'Dunluce. The kitchen is the bit you cannot see, because it is in the sea. Wish you were here. Not for the cooking.'
In the dresser drawer, a recipe card for Bakewell tart with the word 'Pudding' written in capitals and crossed out.
'We make it here in Buxton and we call it tart. If anyone from Bakewell asks, it was a trial run.'
Wedged in a book on walking, a snapshot of the Market Place under snow, in the middle of April, with a man in shorts looking resigned.
The back says: 'Highest market town in England, they say. Grandad insisted on shorts. He caught nothing but a cold.'
At the back of the dresser, a creased map with a long wobbly biro line drawn on it, all the way from the moors to the sea.
In the margin: 'Source to sea, with muddy boots and a flask. Never again. Next year, again.'
Slotted behind a gardening book, a photograph of a woman at a stall in the Pavilion Gardens, a duck waiting patiently by her foot.
Her handwriting underneath reads: 'Ducks run the place. I just sell the cake.'
On the shelf, a small crested china jug with the town's arms on it, no bigger than an egg cup.
Tucked in the spout, a folded note: 'Not for tea. For looking at. Do not mither it.'
Under the bed, a shoebox with a finisher's medal for a hill race, the ribbon fraying and a plaster still stuck to the back.
A note in pen says: 'The Slopes, again. Legs, you are not invited next week.'
Behind the teapot, a photograph of two children holding up fish, the girl's much bigger than the boy's.
On the back, in his handwriting: 'It was the bait.' Underneath, in hers: 'It was not the bait.'
Between two paperbacks, a letter on lined paper from a sister across the water, folded round a recipe.
'Farls sent by the ferry. Eat them hot with butter. Do not tell me how many. I counted what I left.'
Between two old directories, a landlady's rent book with a list of rules in firm capitals.
'No candles. No pets. No cycling indoors.' Underneath, a later hand: 'And no Oxford men before ten.'
In a pile of exercise books, a battered maths notebook with a coffee ring on the cover.
In the margin of the last page: 'Newton did this in a plague year. I have a deadline. Same energy.'
Among the old books, a seven-inch single in a worn paper sleeve, played so often the label has a halo.
Written on it in marker: 'The girl from round the corner. Kept for the voice, not for the shouting.'
On the mantel, a small photograph of a child curled up in a cupboard under the stairs, grinning, with a biscuit.
The back reads: 'The cwtch, the best seat in the house. Washing up is a long way from here.'
On top of the dresser, a velvet rugby cap with a tassel, faded and slightly too small for anyone now living here.
A card pinned to it: 'Our Ffion tried it on last week. Fits her better than the old man. Do not tell him.'
On the shelf, a framed printed ballad sheet of Johnnie Armstrong, the paper yellow, the verses long.
A pencil note on the frame says: 'Family, loosely. Not a role model. Allegedly.'
Hanging on the dresser, an embroidered sampler in faded red wool: three words, a border of thistles, and a very small mistake.
The words are 'Ne oublie.' Someone has stitched underneath, in different thread: 'We do not.'
Propped against the biscuit tin, a school-sized photograph of a gang of kids sitting on the canal bank, all legs and scabs.
In pencil: 'The Bairns, nobody agrees which year. One of them is a stoater. Nobody says which.'
On the dresser, a wooden cheese board with a wire cutter and a handwritten label hanging off the end.
The label says: 'Cheshire, crumbly. Older than your mother's recipes. Cut thin, pretend it was always there.'
Down the side of the sofa, a photograph of a dog on this very sofa, with an expression that says nothing, anywhere, ever happened.
Written on the back: 'Moats do not work on him either. Zoo, take notes.'
Under a pile of takeaway menus, a race card from a day at the Roodee, every horse ticked in biro.
None of them won. In the margin: 'Rood, island, cross, loss. Never again. See you next May.'
On the shelf, an old copy of 'Alice in Wonderland' with a family inscription from a Christmas long ago.
In the margin of the Cheshire Cat page, someone has drawn a grin and written: 'Nobody can prove it.'
Under the clock-shaped trivet, a postcard from a cousin who has gone over the border and not yet come back.
'Annwyl cousin, croeso! I am the one in the hat. The swans here do not take tolls either. Love, ours.'
On the mantel, a black and white photograph of a woman at a wedding, mid-stride, one hip out and chin high.
The back says: 'Nan, in full gatch. Everyone is looking. She is not worried.'
Wedged between the books, a tin whistle with a strip of tape round the middle and a tooth mark in the mouthpiece.
A note in a child's hand: 'The squeaking one. Do NOT call it a yoke.'
On the mantel, a smooth grey pebble sitting in an egg cup, with a label tied round it in blue wool.
'From Blarney. For the gift of the gab. Himself does not need it. Our header definitely does.'
In the display case, a single long lock of Cotswold fleece pinned to a card, wavy and silky and nearly as long as a hand.
The card reads: 'A staple worth a fair. Florence would have paid well. Do not stroke the exhibits.'
On the shelf, a wooden bobbin with a few threads of grey-white linen still wound round it.
The tag says: 'From the mill below. Houl yer whisht and listen, you can still hear it working.'
Between two atlases, a photograph of a small rowing boat on the Foyle at low tide, the mud shining like a tray.
On the back, in a firm hand: 'Out for a walk, 6 pm.' Someone has added an arrow pointing at a dark head in the water. 'Seal. Very polite.'
Behind the clock, a card railway ticket, Derry to Coleraine, punched and kept for no reason anyone will admit.
On the back in pencil: 'Window seat. Sandwiches. Forget the phone.' The household takes this advice seriously.
On the bookshelf, a school photo of the wains sitting in a row on the Walls beside one of the old cannons, squinting into the sun.
One child is clearly mid-sentence. Under the picture: 'Yousens, say cheese. Two of yousens did not.'
Folded into an Irish reader, a page of homework: 'Go raibh maith agat' written twenty times, each one a bit smaller than the last.
On the final line, in a different hand: 'Now say it to your sister.' Underneath, a single defiant 'No.'
In the bookshelf, a summer photograph of a long meadow, mown all round except for a square left standing in the corner.
On the back in biro: 'Their corner.' Below: 'Nobody here has ever seen one. Everybody has heard one at two in the morning.'
Beside the clock hangs an aneroid barometer, tapped every morning before anyone is allowed near a boat.
The needle has sat on 'Change' since before Fungie came to the harbour. A card on the back reads: 'Slán abhaile.'
Kept between two textbooks, a note from a pupil: 'A Mhúinteoir, d'ith mo mhadra m'obair bhaile.' My dog ate my homework.
The reply, in red pen: 'And the cat?' Underneath, the pupil has written: 'The cat does not do Irish.'
Folded flat in the bookshelf, an embroidered sampler: TRAA DY LIOOAR in wobbly cross-stitch, with a sheep below.
The sheep has four horns, because the stitcher, aged nine, was very firm about it. Time enough, indeed.
Inside the clock case, a silver pocket watch in a tobacco tin, stopped at ten past four.
The inscription: 'To Tom from the lads, last sailing.' It loses a minute a day, which is more than the ferry ever did.
Propped on the bookshelf, a blurred photograph of a small dark bird on a washing line, next to a peg.
On the back: 'My one swiftlet. 11.40 on a Tuesday.' Beneath: 'Not telling next door, who have seen none.'
On the shelf, a visitors' book open at a child's entry in felt tip: 'Best bit: the heating under the floor. The Romans had it before us.'
Below it, an adult has added in biro: 'And before our landlord.'
Behind the clock, a staff photograph of clerks lined up under one of the stone river heads, nobody smiling, one looking up at it.
Pencilled on the back: 'Commerce is on the roof. Not pictured. Not working either.'
Tucked into a textbook, a letter from home: 'Your Da says the red and white chimneys are still standing, so you can stop worrying.'
It ends: 'Twenty euro enclosed for a proper dinner, not just tea. Though a sound, deadly cup of tea is also allowed.'
Down the back of the sofa, a child's hurley with the bas wrapped in tape and signed by a whole under-10s team in marker.
The sliotar it was bought for is long gone, probably in a neighbour's garden. Gas altogether.
Folded in the back of the clock, a repair note: 'Mechanism banjaxed. Case lovely. Would advise keeping it as a cabinet.'
Underlined by the owner, firmly: 'Still right twice a day.'
Used as a bookmark in a cookery book, a grease-spotted card in careful handwriting: Gran's barmbrack. 'Soak the fruit in cold tea overnight.'
In pencil at the bottom: 'Mind the ring. Whoever finds it, we'll talk.' The card has clearly seen some baking.
Framed on the shelf, a photograph of the Castle half swallowed by haar, only a flag and one corner of rock showing.
Written on the back: 'Sunny at breakfast.' The grandson says this is proof that the Castle follows him.
On the mantel above the fireplace, a small silver quaich with two handles, polished every January for Burns Night.
A card tucked inside reads: 'For the dram. Not for the gravy.' The neeps, we are told, have heard worse.
Wedged between the sofa cushions, a Fringe programme with nine shows ticked in pencil.
One line reads 'street juggler (free, but we paid anyway)'. A smaller note says 'Wee brother, rehearsing, hide the lamp.'
In the bookshelf, a photograph of the Forth Bridge from the water, long and red against a pale sky, with the new paint gleaming.
On the back: '2011. They finished.' Underneath, in a different pen: 'Told you it would end, Dad.'
Behind the mantel clock, a photograph of Archie aged about six with ice cream down his jumper and his mouth slightly open.
On the back Gran has written 'Glaikit' with great tenderness. The clock beside it is set, naturally, by the One O'Clock Gun.
Stuck in a book on sheep, a postcard from a cousin in Stanley: 'Send diddle-dee jam. Everything here is shop jam.'
Postscript: 'Is the stove still lit?' Pencilled below, in the reply: 'It has not gone out. We have not tested it.'
In the bookshelf, a summer evening photograph of four people on a garden bench in hats and head nets, all smiling like hostages.
The back says: 'Midgies, 8 pm. We lasted eleven minutes.' The bench is still there. The midgies are still there.
Behind the plates, a photograph taken at the Banavie locks: a narrowboat halfway up Neptune's Staircase, a child on the lock beam.
On the back: 'Ninety minutes. Dad timed it.' Pinned next to it is a postcard of the steam train at Glenfinnan, with 'yes, THAT one' scribbled on it.
Pinned between two guidebooks, a thank-you card: 'You found us on the Ben at two in the morning. We cannot say thank you enough.'
Underneath: 'We have bought proper torches. And a map. And we have told someone where we are going.'
Behind the fireplace screen, a tiny cobbler's hammer, about the size of a thumb, resting on a card that says 'For him. Boiler.'
The shoes in the hall still go missing. Nobody has proved the cluricaun innocent.
On the shelf, a photograph of a Galway hooker, black hull, russet sails, tilting hard in a race, a child waving from the quay.
Back of the photo, in felt tip: 'Cruinniú na mBád, Kinvara, August.' The word 'bád' is written three times, in case anyone forgot.
Wrapped in a handkerchief on the shelf, a Claddagh ring: two hands, a heart, a crown, worn almost smooth.
A note pinned to the hanky: 'Mam's. It is not the barmbrack ring. We checked.'
In a dresser drawer, a jam jar of assorted gadgets, labelled in marker: 'YOKES'. Inside: a nutcracker, a thing with a crank, and a key.
A note taped to the lid says: 'The cat likes the one with the crank.' Nobody knows what it does.
Under a pile of marking, one essay kept back and stapled: 'What I did at the weekend: Nothing. It was the best weekend of my life.'
The teacher has written in the margin: 'See me. Also, same.' It is graded an A.
Tucked in the bookshelf, a photograph of the back green: washing lines, a plastic paddling pool, six children and one very serious cat.
On the back: 'Summer. Mind the close door.' The cat is looking directly at the camera and has not forgiven it.
Kept in a book, an orange Subway ticket: the owner rode the whole circle just to say they'd done it.
Pencilled beside it: 'Clockwork Orange. Third oldest in the world. Still dreich.'
On the mantel by the clock, a photograph of a shipyard crew in flat caps under the hull of something enormous, one man circled in biro, holding a flask.
On the back: 'Launch day. Granda circled. He says he held the tea. We have no evidence to the contrary.'
In a cookery book, a recipe card in the family's writing: 'Chicken tikka masala. Invented in Glasgow in the 1970s (allegedly).'
Below, in a different pen: 'Invented in this kitchen in the 1990s (certainly).' A starling outside is practising the ringtone.
Slotted in the shelf, a school jotter where Sundays are spent: a numbered list of Glasgow parks, each one ticked, up to 61.
Beside number 62: 'Park or just a big garden? Ask at the blether.'
Pressed flat in the biggest book on the shelf, a sprig of hawthorn with tiny leaves and a label: 'Holy Thorn, Christmas.'
Another label, in the same hand: 'Do not tell the children it is a hedge.'
Behind the crockery, a photograph of St Michael's Tower on the Tor under snow, taken from the kitchen window.
In the foreground stands the dog, in boots, deeply unimpressed. On the back: 'Gurt big hill. Gurt cold dog.'
Folded in the shelf, a clipboard sheet from last year's clear-up: 'Odd wellies: 212. Tents left behind: too many. Torches: one (mine).'
At the bottom: 'Wispet lights: none seen. Not looking very hard.'
Behind the dresser plates, a black and white photograph of a woman at the door of a thatched blackhouse, a creel on her back, smoke leaking through the roof.
On the back: 'Granny, reading the weather.' Underlined twice: 'Tha i fuar.'
Under a sofa cushion, a revision timetable in four colours: every slot says 'revise' except one that says 'biscuit (essential)'.
The colour-coding was finished a week before any revising began. It is very neat.
On the bookshelf, a tartan shortbread tin holding no shortbread: just recipe cards for cranachan and heather honey labels.
Three generations of handwriting. The tablet card has been left blank on purpose, in case of dentists.
In the bookshelf, a photograph of a grey memorial cairn on open moor, heather in the foreground, tiny walkers at its foot.
On the back: 'Culloden, 1746. Go quietly.' Beneath, in Grandfather's writing: 'Tidy up before bed. Just in case.'
Propped in the dresser, a photograph of a small boat rising in a lock at Muirtown, the water brown and full of sky.
On the back: 'Staircase made of water. 1822 and still going.' The tea ring on the corner is from the same afternoon.
Used as a bookmark, a Highland Games programme with the caber event circled and 'STAND BACK' in capitals.
A child's pencil has added: 'Hootlet by the churchyard again. It sounded like our doorbell.'
Behind the clock, an undated photograph of a carter handing coins through the tollhouse hatch, his horse gazing at the river.
On the back: 'Free since 1950. The horse never paid anyway.'
In the display case, a screw-top jar of groatie buckies, tiny shells from the shore, each picked over for a perfect ridge.
The label: 'Last jar of the season. Haste ye back.' Kept for luck, not for sale, as long as nobody offers enough.
On the dresser, a small carving of a stag in bog oak, black as coal, antlers worn pale by thumbs.
A scrap tucked underneath says: 'Roars in autumn. Sure look it.' Which is the whole of Kerry philosophy.
In the guest book, an entry in green ink: 'Best drying room in the Lakes. Our boots have never been happier.'
The next guest has added: 'Castlerigg at dawn. Thirty-eight stones and no signal. Perfect.'
In the bookshelf, a photograph of a nearly black newborn lamb on a stone wall, its grey mother standing watch behind.
Written underneath: 'Fades with age.' Someone has added: 'Like us.'
Propped on the dresser, a photograph of a small child in a cardboard tree costume with felt leaves, one arm raised mid-whoosh.
The programme next to it credits 'Tree'. Dad has added, in pen: 'Best tree. Ever.'
On the shelf, a slate coaster engraved with BECK, FELL, TARN and YAT, a glossary for visitors who ask for 'the gate'.
Beside it, a notebook of osprey notes: 'Day 11: osprey! Opened a bottle. It was ten in the morning.'
Behind the clock, an engraved slate coaster: a thank-you from a family the mountain rescue team once brought down safe.
The back says 'Pack a torch.' Dinner has been kept warm under it more than once.
Between two cookbooks, a photograph of a small, stern Dexter cow at a show, rosette pinned to her halter.
On the back: 'Moolet, 2nd place. Judge was your man from Carlow. We will not be speaking of it.'
Propped by the hearth, a child's hurley, scuffed pale at the bas. The big one over the fire is Granda's, this is its understudy.
Touched for luck before every match. The record on results is, being honest, mixed.
Down the back of the sofa, a letter from a sister in Galway. 'The yoke is banjaxed again, send help or a screwdriver.'
P.S. 'Tell Mam the otter story is true. I have seen the droppings. They smell of tea.'
Under the pillow, a black and amber scarf, washed thin from forty summers of standing in the rain at Croke Park.
The knot has never been undone. A granddaughter claims it, and loses it, on a rolling basis.
On the shelf, a jam jar of sea glass, green, white and one rare blue, each with a scrap of paper: 'tideline, a calm Tuesday'.
A note on the lid: 'Not for swapping. Well. Ask nicely.'
Folded into a book on the Flow, a letter from a cousin who dives: 'Cold, green, and the wrecks are enormous. You feel you are trespassing.'
He signs off: 'Come south and I will get you a drysuit. Do not argue, you will love it.'
On the mantel, a photograph of a Ba' Game scrum on Christmas Day, steam rising off a hundred backs, the ball somewhere in the middle.
In biro on the back: 'Dad in there, we think. Third from the left, possibly the elbow.'
Slipped into a guidebook, a faded postcard of the Skara Brae houses with the stone dressers still in place.
Written on it: 'Dusting is easy here. Wish I could say the same at home. Back Friday.'
In a dresser drawer among the string and the rubber bands, a worn sheepdog whistle on a bootlace.
Teeth marks on the mouthpiece. The dog has been blamed for them. The dog has not confessed.
Under a cushion, a photograph of a line of walkers crossing the Bay sands behind the guide, wellies and all.
Written beneath: 'Kept to the guide's heels. Tide came in an hour later and we were on the far side, toasting it.'
In a cookbook, a recipe in a neat hand: 'Hotpot. Potatoes sliced thin, overlapped like roof slates. Do not mither it.'
Underneath, in a different pen: 'It is better the second day. This is a fact, not an opinion.'
On the dresser rail, a painted Roses and Castles jug, the kind that decorated narrowboat cabins, chipped but loved.
Scratched under the base: 'Home, wherever the mooring.' Still says 'aboard' for 'come in'.
Under the bed, a child's drawing of a bin lorry with a big red rose on its side, captioned 'The County Bin'.
Pinned to it: 'Our Jack, age 6. Framed, then unframed after the Thursday fox incident.'
Folded in a drawer under the bed, a fine lace shawl, light enough to pull through a wedding ring, wrapped in tissue.
A card: 'Played at her wedding till the sun was up. Never did stop humming.'
In a velvet box between the leather spines, a Claddagh ring: hands, heart and crown, worn smooth.
The note says: 'Heart toward you means spoken for. Heart outward, ask politely.' The fox has not offered an opinion.
Tucked in a history, a letter from a school class: 'Thank you for telling us about 1290. We did not know it was so close to home.'
A drawing of the house is pinned beside it, with one wobbly door. The teacher has underlined 'remember'.
In the dresser drawer, a recipe card in Mam's hand: 'Scouse. Lamb, spuds, onions. Pan on low. Do not hurry. Do not call it stew.'
A grease thumbprint in the corner has become part of the recipe.
Behind the clock, a yellowing telegram: 'Docked safe Wednesday. Love to all. Put the kettle on.'
Pinned with the wage slip that proves it was the only time he sent a message that short.
Between folders, a photograph of the Overhead Railway running above the dock road, a wet day and a line of lorries below.
The caption: 'The Dockers' Umbrella. Project notes at the back. Still need a good ending.'
Down the side of the sofa, a worn seven-inch single in a paper sleeve, signed 'To Hope Street' in felt tip.
Never played in front of guests. Played every other day when they have gone.
Inside a tea tin on the clock shelf, a coin hoard marked 'Our Jack: ferry across the Mersey'.
Nan has been topping it up with pound coins and has added a lolly stick: 'Interest'.
Pinned inside the dresser door, a grainy photograph of the warehouse from the 1900s, carts out front and the cast-iron pillars just visible.
Someone has written 'No wood, no fire' in pencil, and then 'Fingers crossed'.
On the mantelpiece, a brass miner's lamp polished to a shine, next to a homemade one with a slate back.
A scrap of card: 'Forty years on the mountain. Knees remember. Lamp too.'
Between the picture books, a crayon drawing of a stage and a crowd, labelled in wobbly letters: 'HWYL'.
Below it, in adult handwriting: 'Eisteddfod practice, 7pm. She sang the whole thing twice.'
Propped on the mantel, a black-and-white photograph of a small quarry loco on the lake line, steam up, a man waving.
On the back: 'Small and stubborn. Both of them. Hiraeth, even then.'
Under the bed, a race number safety-pinned to a muddy vest, from a run up the long route to the summit.
The pin is bent. The finishing time on the back is crossed out and written again, smaller.
In the dresser drawer, a photograph of a gang of quarrymen in their caban, flat caps and tin mugs, one fellow pulling a face.
Back of the print: 'Grandad, middle, with the whistle. Dinner at twelve, no argument.'
In a drawer-sized book, a typed letter from the quarry, 1969, with a handwritten line at the bottom from the foreman.
It reads: 'Sorry, lad.' The reply was never sent. The envelope is kept anyway.
Wrapped in a tea towel, a Welsh lovespoon, a heart carved into the handle, dated in biro on the tag.
The note: 'Made by a cousin who cannot whittle. The heart is a bit lopsided. That is the charm.'
At the back of the dresser drawer, windlass number eight, which nobody knew existed.
A label on it: 'Found. Do not tell the others. Put it with the seven you lost.'
Under a cushion, a photograph of a man in a thick woolly jumper on a beach in July, scowling at the sunshine.
In pen: 'Nesh. Told you.' And, smaller: 'Ice cream was not offered. Mardy.'
On the shelf, a flattened Hovis bread bag from years back, kept for the colours and a note on the inside.
It says: 'Named in Macclesfield. Strength of man, strength of toast.' Dad has added a smiley face.
In a biscuit tin, a wooden silk mill bobbin, wound with a few turns of faded thread.
The label: 'Mum's, from the mill. Soft hands, she said, or it would snag.'
Beside the clock, a framed photograph of a figure on a pointed summit in anorak and sunshine, a flask raised.
The caption: 'Shutlingsloe, again. The Matterhorn, allegedly. Packed lunch: yes.'
Hung on a nail inside the dresser door, a polished horse brass, the sort that jangled on canal towpath horses.
A scrap of paper: 'Roving bridge, 1831 and every year since. Horse never had to be unhitched.'
Pressed between the pages of Gran's recipe book, a bundle of dried flowers, labelled in her hand with names and dates.
'Elderflower, June. Rowan, September. Hands washed before touching.' Good advice, honestly.
In a drawer under the bed, an enamel badge of a worker bee, slightly chipped, pinned to a card.
'Graft, our kid.' Hand-written: 'Wear it on a Friday. Bees do not take holidays.'
Down the sofa, a telly remote held together with brown tape and a note: 'DO NOT LOSE. Last one in the house.'
Dad has added: 'First stored-program computer 1948. This remote, 1994. Equally mysterious.'
Between two textbooks, a card from Mum with a tenner inside. 'Eat something that is not toast. Rutherford did not split atoms on toast.'
The tenner is long gone. The card is still here, to be fair.
On the dresser, a Coronation biscuit tin, lid dented. Opened, it holds buttons, not Eccles cakes, which is the great disappointment.
Nana's note: 'Hands off. Cakes are in the other tin.'
In a book, a ribbon in purple, white and green, folded neatly in a paper wrapper.
Written on the wrapper: 'The colours of Nelson Street. Keep them where the front room can see.'
Behind the clock, a photograph of a man in a flat cap standing outside a brick mill in the drizzle, umbrella on his arm.
'Good for the thread, bad for the hair', says the back, in marker pen.
On the mantel, a note on the back of an envelope: 'Owt for tea? Nowt in. Get owt. Not chips again. Chips again.'
Beneath it, a drawing of a narrowboat and the instruction 'Moor on time'.
Folded in sheet music, a petition: 'We the neighbours kindly request cornet practice end before nine.' Four signatures, one a smiley.
The daughter has replied below in felt tip: 'Noted. Practising the quiet one.'
Between two books, a postcard from a cousin abroad: 'Only a cúpla focal left, but I say them to the kettle every morning.'
It ends: 'Slán go fóill. Mind the crex crex for me.'
On the shelf, a trowel worn down to a stump of steel, with a tag in marker: 'Fifteen summers.'
Beside it, a sticker from the first dig: 'Ask me about spirals. Then ask me again, I will have a new guess.'
Between two books, a photograph of Granda with a horse and plough, a flat field and a hawthorn hedge behind him.
'Flint on every furrow', the back reads. 'The field was winning.'
On the mantel, a photograph of the same crooked picture, taken by someone who had clearly tried to straighten it first.
On the back: 'On the huh. Always has been. Leave it, bor.'
On the shelf, a flint nodule split by hand, black and glassy as a wet pebble inside, a rough chalk-white skin outside.
A label: 'Knapped on the beach. Took six goes and one thumb.'
Tucked down the sofa, a photograph of three friends under a stone lion at the Council House, all squinting into the sun.
The back says: 'Meet at the Left Lion. 1pm. Do not be late, me duck.'
Between two paperbacks on the shelf, a match photograph gone brown at the edges: a roaring crowd, one scarf circled in biro.
On the back, in careful capitals: 'Me, 1979. Do not lose.' The scarf, you suspect, is still around here somewhere.
Propped against the teapot in the dresser, a note in felt tip: 'Mum, I have gone to bed. I left you a cob. I did not say please.'
Underneath, in smaller letters: 'Hootlet has not moved. Is that normal?' A night nurse's household, in one sheet of paper.
Wedged behind a row of Sillitoe and Lawrence, a single typewriter key, the letter S, worn smooth by somebody's thumb.
A scrap of paper with it says 'Found at a car boot. Probably nothing to do with Nottingham. Probably.' It is a Typewriter Key, and a hopeful one.
On the mantelpiece, behind the candlestick, a black and white photograph of the quay with a ferry half out of the frame.
The back says 'First one I counted, 1958. Stood too close.' Nothing since has been counted, but everything has been watched.
In the dresser drawer, a folded team sheet from a Saturday match: twelve names in blotchy pencil, one crossed out.
Beside the crossed-out name someone has written 'broken wrist' and then, more bitterly, 'but he still turned up to watch'.
Pinned inside the dresser door, a lost property list in a hurried hand: one hat, one shoe, one phone, one wedding ring.
At the bottom: 'Plus one pole, returned by a man who said it was not his fault. They always say that.'
On the dresser, wrapped in a tea towel, a Fresnel prism: a thick wedge of glass that throws a rainbow across the wall at noon.
The household swears it came off the lighthouse lens during a service. Nobody has paperwork, and nobody is asking.
In the dresser drawer, a recipe card in pencil, grease-spotted at one corner: 'Nan's pasty. Crimp on the side, not the top.'
A hag stone on a bit of string hangs beside it, the hole big enough to see through. The card adds, 'Do the crimp dreckly. It will keep.'
Behind a row of tide tables, a photograph of a boat nosing into Newlyn harbour, PZ painted on the bow and gulls over every rail.
A thumb has left a mark across one corner. On the back: 'Home before the weather. For once.'
On the dresser sits Dad's brass miner's lamp, polished so often the pattern has worn off the lid.
Beside it, on a saucer, is a small pasty crust. Nobody in the house will say who it is for, but it is changed every week.
Tucked behind a seaside paperback, a snapshot of a man in a bobble hat standing waist-deep in the Jubilee Pool in January.
He is grinning with the grin of someone who has stopped feeling anything. The caption reads 'Proper job. Dad, aged brave.'
Pinned to a roof beam, a photograph of a longboat crew mid-surf, every oar pointing in a different direction.
On the back, in the old cox's slanting hand: 'Two out of three. Do not ask which two.'
In the stewards' cupboard, taped under a shelf: a cup tie programme, the green cover soft as cloth from handling.
Someone has circled the team sheet and written 'We lost, but we sang'. It reads like the club motto, if a club could be that honest.
Slid inside a cookbook, a card in a neat hand: 'Mòran taing for the scones. And for the second scones.'
On the back is a tally: nine scones, three of them 'for the road'. Whoever lives here is clearly a person other people go out of their way to thank.
Beside the clock, an aneroid barometer in a dark wood case. Its needle has pointed at 'Change' since the spring.
Under it, a tag reads 'Tap gently. Do not believe a word it says about the Minch.' The household keeps it out of loyalty.
On the shelf, a Gaelic phrasebook with pencilled sounds above the hard words: 'madainn mhath' has a little 'matt-in va' scribbled over it.
On the flyleaf, 'Oidhche mhath' is written out eleven times, each one a bit more confident.
Under the pillow, a printed photograph of a small child standing inside a huge dinosaur footprint at Staffin, arms out like a referee.
The child is bundled in a coat three sizes too big. On the back: 'For the school project. I am tiny. That was the point.'
Folded under the scales, a note on chapel paper: 'Rehearsal Tuesday, second row, tenors early. Bring Welsh cakes. Elwyn.'
Under the signature somebody has added, in pencil, 'Especially bring Welsh cakes.' The choir's priorities are clear.
On the dresser, among the good china, a miniature tin bath no bigger than a loaf, hung with a loop of string.
The household calls it 'the Friday one'. Whoever put it up has also scratched 'First in!' into the base, which is probably a joke.
Behind the clock, in a cloth bag, a silver pocket watch with a dent on the case and a ferry timetable folded inside the lid.
The timetable is from the days before the 1966 bridge. The watch has not been wound since, which is more than can be said for the ferryman.
In the dresser drawer, a note in a boy's handwriting: 'To whom it may concern: I will be riding the Severn bore on Saturday.'
Below, in a parent's firm hand: 'You will be riding the bath first. Hafren will wait.'
Propped at the back of the dresser, a black and white photograph of a half-door, top open to the yard, a hen sitting calmly on the bottom half.
Behind the hen, a woman is laughing mid-sentence at someone off the edge of the picture. It is not clear whether the hen or the pig started it.
Behind a stack of school books, a snapshot of the youngest, holding a paper bag of 'spice' in one hand and a football in the other.
Two front teeth are missing. The back says 'Sheffield for sweets. Not curry. We have explained this to the whole street.'
Down the back of the sofa cushions, a single child's goalkeeping glove, pegged-up fingers still stiff from the washing line.
Its pair is, the household suspects, in the next garden. Sheffield FC began in 1857, and still nobody in this house can find the other glove.
Stuck to the front of the clock, a yellow sticky note: 'That ringing is the starlet. It is NOT me. Do not answer it.'
It is signed with a heavy underline. Half the street has stopped picking up, and at least one neighbour has begun to reply 'hello' to a bird.
Behind the clock, tucked in the frame, the husband's old clocking-in card from the steelworks, soft with years of pocket.
Scrawled across the back in pencil: 'Tha's late.' The household maintains this was not meant as a criticism.
Under the bed, in a biscuit tin lid, a sheepdog whistle on a leather bootlace, the metal dulled to the colour of the loch.
It is blown once, and a very old dog on the other side of the wall gets up with a groan. The household claims he is deaf.
Wrapped in greaseproof paper in the dresser, a lucky sixpence with a label: 'Brack, Hallowe'en. Found by Auntie Peggy, who gave out about it.'
The ring from the barmbrack was never recovered. Auntie Peggy maintains that the sixpence is a lesser prize, and has said so for decades.
Slipped behind the book spines, a photograph of a very old tortoise crossing a lawn with the air of a man late for a meeting.
A caption in a governor's looping hand: 'Right of way. Always.' The lawn, as promised, is spotless.
Under the tea caddy, a postcard of the cliffs written in blue biro: 'Wish you were here. A gwylan took my chips and my dignity.'
It is signed 'Your cousin' with a small drawing of a gull looking smug. No stamp. It was clearly never sent, only enjoyed.
On the dresser, a lovespoon carved by hand, the bowl cut with a fish and a little cross-hatched wave.
Carved on the back in tiny letters is 'Ynys Dewi'. The household says it was made for a courtship, and then adds, 'Sort of. It was a long courtship.'
Stuck between two school books, a page headed 'St David' in a child's wobbly hand: 'He lived on bread and water. I could do this.'
Underneath, a late addendum: 'Please send more bread. Cai.' The teacher has written 'Noted' in green pen.
In the dresser drawer, a dessert spoon with a strip of masking tape on the handle: 'Return to this house. We mean it.'
Four more spoons are in the drawer beneath, each with its own strip. Nobody has ever returned one, but the lobby keeps getting made.
On the shelf, a family snapshot on the terraces: dad, his dad, the children, everyone in a scarf and everyone mid-yell.
Written below in a shaky hand: 'Burslem. Not a choice, a condition.' The baby in the front looks utterly uninterested in the football.
Behind the plates on the dresser, a brightly painted saucer, a pattern of orange and yellow in sharp, cheerful stripes.
The placer says it was a 'second', which means a flaw somewhere. After an hour of staring, the household still cannot find it.
Between two grammars, a pack of hand-written flashcards held with a hairband. The top one reads 'Am bheil thu sgìth?', and on the back, 'Tha.'
The next card says 'Chan eil.' The pack has been through many hands, and the corners are soft as cloth.
A black and white photograph in a cracked frame: a crowd of herring girls on a quay, sleeves rolled, knives flashing, mouths wide open in song.
On the back, in a fisherman's hand: 'Faster than the knife, some of them.' No one has ever disagreed.
Used as a bookmark, a postcard of the lighthouse: 'Windy. The salt ponds are pink. The sea looks like a blue tablecloth. Love to all.'
Beneath that, in a different pen, 'Hat now in the sea.' The sender has clearly relaxed into the holiday.
On the dresser, a slab of Caithness flagstone with the ghost of a fish pressed into it, scales like fine stitching.
The label reads 'Out on the hills by noon. Found it before the glasses.' The baker's habits are, it seems, a family tradition.
In the dresser drawer, an unsent Christmas card with a robin on it: 'Dear Keiths. Peace? Gunns.'
It has been written, rewritten, and put back every winter. The stamp has fallen off. So, in a sense, has the feud.
Tucked behind the kettle on the dresser, a photograph of the marsh in flood at a high autumn tide, the grass drowned and the birds piled onto what is left.
Someone has written a note on the back: 'Short-eared owl, left of the post. Honestly. No, left.'
In the dresser, a small cardboard ticket gone brown with age: Hooton to West Kirby, from before the line became a path.
The household keeps it in an old tobacco tin with a note: 'Never had to wait for it. Now we wait for the dog.'
Used as a bookmark, a laundry ticket stub: 'Tablecloths, Tuesday. Damp. Smells faintly of brook.'
Next to the word 'brook' there is a long crossed-out line. Whoever lives here is a poor liar and a very thorough launderer.
Stuck behind the clock, a tide table for the Dee with every high water ringed in pencil, and a cross beside the dangerous ones.
In the margin: 'Never on the marsh without checking.' Under it, smaller: 'Pupplash fed again. Do not tell.'
On the shelf, a thumbed-to-death paperback of city walks, a folded map tucked inside with every snickelway pencilled in.
A note on the flyleaf: 'Mind your head on the beam. And on the next three.' The map is more used than the book.
Under a pile of paperbacks, a scrap of envelope: 'What is for tea?' 'Nowt.' 'Right.'
The answer is signed with a flourish. The household has been having this conversation since long before anyone dug up Coppergate.
Between two paperbacks, a dented Coronation biscuit tin, now holding flattened foil wrappers from chocolate oranges of Christmases past.
Each wrapper has a year in pencil. The bairn is under strict instructions not to eat the lid.
